Anderson RM.lab_name: Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Anderson RM.role: Professor of medicine at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies the basic biology of aging and how calorie restriction slows it, and senior author of the 2017 comparison of the two long-running rhesus monkey calorie restriction studies
Anderson RM.sub: Professor, Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison · Health Officer, Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital, Madison · earlier: postdoctoral fellow, UW-Madison Institute on Aging · postdoctoral fellow, Harvard Medical School (David Sinclair's group, papers 2002–2003) · PhD in biochemistry, University College Dublin
story: Rozalyn Anderson was senior author of a 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that resolved an apparent conflict between two of the longest experiments in aging research. One group at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin had followed rhesus monkeys on calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, for decades. Wisconsin had reported longer survival and the NIA had not. Analysing both studies side by side, the paper found consistent health benefits in both, and showed that the survival effect depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed.

Calorie restriction is the oldest known way to slow aging in animals, and lower mTORC1 activity is one of the routes through which it is thought to work. Monkeys are much closer to humans than mice are, so this comparison is among the strongest primate evidence that eating less improves health. It leaves open how large any lifespan gain would be.

Anderson earned a PhD in biochemistry at University College Dublin. As a postdoctoral fellow in David Sinclair's group at Harvard Medical School she worked on calorie restriction in yeast, and in 2003 she was first author of papers in Nature and Science showing that the enzyme PNC1, which removes nicotinamide, is needed for calorie restriction to extend yeast lifespan, and that this effect does not depend on swings in the cell's NAD+ to NADH ratio. A second postdoctoral fellowship at the UW-Madison Institute on Aging moved her to the mechanisms by which calorie restriction delays aging in mammals. She is now a professor in the Division of Geriatrics and Gerontology of the Department of Medicine, a faculty member of the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, and Health Officer at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the Madison VA hospital. Her lab asks why aging makes people more vulnerable to cancer, diabetes, heart disease and neurodegeneration. Recent papers cover how calorie restriction remodels the mouse brain, how an acetyl-CoA transporter in the endoplasmic reticulum changes neuron metabolism, and sex differences in aging.

Brignole EJ.lab_name: MIT Cryo-EM Facility, MIT.nano, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Brignole EJ.role: Research scientist who directs the cryo-electron microscopy facility at MIT.nano and whose cryo-EM work helped solve the structures of GATOR1, GATOR2 and Raptor docked on the Rag GTPases for the Sabatini lab
Brignole EJ.sub: Director, MIT cryo-EM facility at MIT.nano (appointed 2017) · research scientist in Catherine Drennan's lab, MIT (from 2010)
story: Edward Brignole is a co-author of three structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, all made with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In cryo-EM, purified proteins are frozen in a thin layer of ice and photographed thousands of times with an electron beam, and the images are combined into a 3D model. The method needs careful sample preparation and microscope work, which is where an EM specialist comes in.

The three papers solve key parts of how mTORC1 senses amino acids. SHE2018 gives the structure of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rag GTPases off, alone and bound to the Rags, and shows how it does so. ROG2019 shows how Raptor, part of mTORC1, docks onto the Rag-Ragulator complex on the lysosome: one part of Raptor reads the state of RagA and a separate claw reads RagC, and only the right combination lets mTORC1 land. VAL2022 gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex built on an octagonal frame, and maps where the sensors Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 attach. How GATOR2 holds back GATOR1 is still not fully settled.

Brignole joined Catherine Drennan's lab at MIT in 2010 as a research scientist and worked mainly on ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes the building blocks of DNA; the PubMed record shows fifteen joint papers with the Drennan group up to 2023. In late 2017 the Drennan lab announced that Brignole had been appointed to direct MIT's new cryo-EM facility, housed in the MIT.nano building, while keeping up the work with the lab. Running a shared facility means helping groups across MIT, such as the Sabatini lab, turn purified proteins into 3D structures, which is how the Atlas papers came about.

Lovat P.lab_name: Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Lovat P.role: Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology at Newcastle University who studies autophagy in melanoma, and whose work on the autophagy protein AMBRA1 and the skin protein loricrin underlies a test, developed with AMLo Biosciences, to identify early melanomas at low risk of spreading
Lovat P.sub: Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology, Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University · Chief Scientific Officer, AMLo Biosciences, Newcastle upon Tyne
story: Penny Lovat is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Viktor Korolchuk's lab at Newcastle University on why ageing cells behave as they do. CAR2017 showed that in senescent human cells (cells that have permanently stopped dividing) mTORC1, the growth-control complex, stays switched on even when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals, and the cells come to depend on this signal to survive. KEL2024 showed that healthy human cells constantly recycle damaged mitochondria (basal mitophagy), that this stops when cells become senescent, and that part of rapamycin's anti-ageing effect on cells needs mitophagy to be restored. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Lovat's own research centres on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in skin cancer. PubMed lists her at Newcastle University on more than 50 papers on melanoma and autophagy. Her group found that the autophagy regulator AMBRA1 and the skin barrier protein loricrin are lost from the skin above melanomas that are more likely to spread. With collaborators in Rome she showed that the HPV virus breaks down AMBRA1 in throat cancers, which lowers autophagy and makes the tumour cells easier to kill with cisplatin (2020). A 2026 study tested AMBRA1 and loricrin staining to help pathologists tell high-grade moles from thin melanomas.

Lovat is Professor of Cellular Dermatology and Oncology at Newcastle University and Chief Scientific Officer of AMLo Biosciences, the Newcastle company that brings the AMBRA1 and loricrin test to clinical use. PubMed papers list her at the university's Translational and Clinical Research Institute.
sources: PubMed search Lovat P[Author] AND (melanoma OR autophagy)

Fuchs H.lab_name: German Mouse Clinic, Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich (Neuherberg, Germany)
Fuchs H.role: Scientific and technical head of the German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich, the standardised many-organ testing platform for mouse models that Fuchs helped build
Fuchs H.sub: Scientific and Technical Head, German Mouse Clinic, Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich (since 2001) · Dysmorphology Screen, Munich ENU Mouse Mutagenesis Project (1997–2001) · doctorate in agricultural sciences, Technical University of Munich
story: Helmut Fuchs is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Fuchs studied agricultural sciences at the Technical University of Munich and did a doctorate on genetic diversity and evolution in local fish populations. After joining Helmholtz Munich in 1997, Fuchs ran the Dysmorphology Screen of the Munich ENU mouse mutagenesis project, which produced more than 400 mutant mouse lines. From 2000 Fuchs helped build the German Mouse Clinic with Valerie Gailus-Durner and Martin Hrabě de Angelis, setting up what the institute describes as the first mouse phenotyping pipeline in the world, and has been its scientific and technical head since 2001. The clinic tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems, and Fuchs also chairs working groups in the European Infrafrontier network and the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium. Research interests include bone metabolism, genes that affect several traits at once, and how to design and analyse large phenotyping studies. Recent examples are a 2026 analysis of heart weight in more than 25,000 mice from the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium and a 2026 mouse model of a genetic movement disorder, KMT2B-related dystonia.

Waickman AT.lab_name: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (Syracuse, New York, USA)
Waickman AT.role: Immunologist who trained in Jonathan Powell's mTOR and T cell lab at Johns Hopkins and now studies human immune responses to dengue virus at SUNY Upstate Medical University
Waickman AT.sub: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (2025 Upstate news, 2026 PubMed affiliation) · Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, around 2011–2016)
story: Adam Waickman appears in this Atlas on two papers from Jonathan Powell's laboratory at Johns Hopkins that split T cell decisions between the two mTOR complexes. The 2011 Nature Immunology paper showed that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages. The 2015 Journal of Clinical Investigation paper did the same for killer (CD8) T cells: constant mTORC1 activity, after deleting Tsc2, produced aggressive but short-lived effector cells with no memory, while removing mTORC1 activity by deleting Rheb gave memory-like cells that still responded poorly to a second encounter with the antigen.

In the same period Waickman co-authored a 2015 PLoS One study from the lab showing that, within one batch of freshly activated CD4 T cells, the larger cells with high mTOR activity become glycolytic effector cells, while the smaller cells with low mTOR activity tend to become long-lived cells and regulatory T cells, a pattern also seen in human T cells.

PubMed lists close to 70 papers under Waickman's name. The recent ones come from the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at SUNY Upstate Medical University in Syracuse and deal with human immunity to dengue virus, including a 2026 Lancet Microbe report on a first-in-human dengue serotype 4 challenge study run with the University of Maryland and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research. In 2025 Upstate announced a 3.1 million dollar NIH grant for Waickman to study how a second dengue infection becomes life-threatening and to build tools for better dengue diagnosis, vaccines and patient care.

Marchant ED.lab_name: Rasmussen Lab, Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Marchant ED.role: Graduate student in Blake Rasmussen's lab in San Antonio who studies what overactive mTORC1 in skeletal muscle does to metabolism, inflammation and exercise adaptation in aging and overnutrition
Marchant ED.sub: Graduate student, Biology of Aging discipline, Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, UT Health San Antonio (Rasmussen lab) · MS in nutritional science, Brigham Young University (2022) · BS in nutritional science, Brigham Young University (2019)
story: Erik Marchant is first author of the Atlas study MARCHANT2026, with B. B. Rasmussen as senior author. Overactive mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in muscle is often linked with insulin resistance, the state in which the body handles sugar poorly. To test whether one causes the other, the team switched mTORC1 on permanently in mouse skeletal muscle by removing GATOR1, a protein complex that normally turns mTORC1 off when amino acids are scarce.

The muscles showed more signs of inflammation, but the mice still handled a glucose load normally. So muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone was not enough to cause glucose intolerance, and other metabolic inputs must be needed. A companion paper from the same group in 2026, with Marchant as second author, found that this kind of hyperactive muscle mTORC1 blunted the benefits of endurance training even though mitochondria and lipids changed. Both studies are in mice.

Marchant earned a bachelor's degree (2019) and a master's degree (2022) in nutritional science at Brigham Young University in Utah. Papers from that time include a 2020 study showing that, unlike a high-fat diet, bed rest did not appear to cause insulin resistance through mitochondrial oxidants, and a 2018 commentary on restricting branched-chain amino acids for metabolic health. Marchant is now a graduate student in the Biology of Aging discipline at UT Health San Antonio, in the lab of Blake Rasmussen, working on muscle metabolism in aging and overnutrition. Besides the mTORC1 work, the projects include testing ultrasound as a possible treatment for insulin resistance in old mice, and co-authored human studies of muscle disuse and rehabilitation in middle-aged adults (2025) and of PDE-5 inhibitors (2026).

Goul C.lab_name: Leonetti Group, Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Goul C.role: Cell biologist who did graduate work in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley on lysosomes and mTORC1, first author of a major review of how mTORC1 senses nutrients and of a 2026 Nature study on how damaged lysosomes are repaired, now a scientist at CZ Biohub
Goul C.sub: Scientist, Leonetti group, Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco · graduate student, Zoncu lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (papers 2022–2026)
story: Claire Goul was first author of a 2023 review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (GOU2023) that explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, senses nutrients. mTORC1 is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when amino acids, glucose, cholesterol and growth signals are all present, and it then drives the making of proteins, fats and new cell parts. The review walks through the sensors and switches involved, including the Rag GTPases that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, and how faults in this system contribute to metabolic disease, cancer and other conditions. It is a good entry point for a reader who wants the whole pathway in one place.

Goul's research in Roberto Zoncu's lab centres on the lysosome. In 2022 Goul co-wrote a short Developmental Cell commentary on lysosome repair, and in 2026 was first author of a Nature paper describing LASER, which links the sensing of lysosome damage to the assembly of the ESCRT machinery that patches the membrane. Goul also co-authored a 2025 EMBO Journal study showing that autophagosomes anchor a checkpoint that shapes PKA signalling in neurons.

Goul did this work as a graduate student in the Zoncu lab, which lists Goul among its alumni. After leaving Berkeley, Goul became a scientist in the Leonetti group at the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub in San Francisco.
